resources.string: Its settings and all its learned sequences are deleted. This cannot be undone.
Stop the exercise to change its settings.
Each mode keeps its own learned sequences.
Time from one step to the next.
How long the app holds its note, in percent of the breathing time.
How hard the app strikes its notes (1–127).
At least %1$s semitones. Exercises start at %2$s.
How often each interval is chosen for a random step (0 = never).
Give at least one interval a weight above 0.
Share of the steps that replay a sequence you got wrong before (%1$s stored for this mode).
Stored with the setup; the exercise does not use it yet (neither did the Java version).
When you play a step wrong, the steps before it are stored and come back later.
Stored with the setup; the exercise does not use it yet (neither did the Java version).
%1$s of them reach outside the current range and are skipped until the range covers them again.
New mistakes start at level 1. Each time a sequence is practised it moves one level on, and after the last level it is forgotten. Lower levels come back more often.
Forget all sequences of this mode…
All learned sequences of the mode “%1$s” in this setup are deleted.
Notes you play are recognised at any time.
Without headphones the microphone hears the app too: while the app plays a note, that note and its octaves are ignored.

Without headphones the microphone hears the app too. With “%1$s” as MIDI Out the app removes its own sound, so every note counts (it needs a few notes at the start of an exercise to learn your room; until then the note the app is playing and its octaves are ignored while it sounds).
Right notes in another octave count
The recognition mistakes octaves far more often than you do (a piano’s low notes have weak fundamentals).
A note you strike up to this long after the next note has started still answers the note before, if that had no answer yet.
Relative to the reference A. The level bar should move clearly when you play.
A keyboard you plug in becomes the input right away. Devices are opened when you press Start.
“%1$s” plays samples of the Salamander Grand Piano by Alexander Holm (CC BY 3.0).
“%1$s” is played by the app itself, so it can remove its sound from the microphone signal.
“Test MIDI” shows the keys arriving from MIDI In; “Play test note” plays A′ on MIDI Out, tuned to the reference A.
Shifts the whole output by a pitch bend; applied immediately, also during an exercise.
These settings only apply to microphone input.
Saves the microphone signal (WAV, about 5 MB per minute) and a log of the notes played and recognised to %1$s, to tune the recognition with real sound.
For tuning the recognition: every exercise stops by itself after a number of notes and is recorded; afterwards the Practice screen lists each step, so you can report where you played something else.
Off: while the app plays a note, that note and its octaves are ignored instead (for comparison).
Chord recognition for %1$s voices (the exercise’s mode), set apart from single notes.
On: which partials are there, after levelling out the room (robust to where the microphone stands). Off: how the spectrum’s shape matches note templates (best right after a calibration).
Not calibrated: the chord recognition uses a piano model.
Calibrating asks for every note of the range (%1$s – %2$s) once: play each alone, with the sustain pedal up; the app plays nothing meanwhile.
Heard %1$s – please play the asked note again.
Minimum level of a stroke (RMS, full scale 1).
How much a stroke must raise the level above the moments before it.
How periodic a window must be for its pitch to count.
Analysis windows that must agree on the note.
Lower: fewer octave-down errors, more octave-up errors.
Safety factor on the app’s predicted own sound.
Slowest decay of the own sound per 11.6 ms (the room’s reverberation).
Over the app’s sound, a stroke must raise the total level by this factor.
Where the app’s note starts, a stroke must exceed this share of it.
Until the own sound is learned, strokes must be this many times louder than the microphone while the app plays.
Within 400 ms after a recognised note, a new stroke over the app’s sound must raise the level by this factor (against beating).
How long after a stroke the spectrum is averaged (ms): longer separates bass notes better.
Strokes this close together (ms) are one chord.
Higher: prefers fewer notes (against extra notes; too high misses notes).
A note must carry this share of a chord’s energy to count.
Above 0 leans towards “played as given” (fewer false mistakes, more missed ones).
How much of what rang before the stroke is removed.
Share of the level that must be new (against beating of close notes).
Harmonic: width (semitones) of the envelope that levels out the room’s colouring.
Harmonic: a partial counts as there this many times above its surroundings.
Harmonic: per expected partial that is not there (settles octaves).
Harmonic: how much a deep note’s dense partials are discounted for catching peaks by chance.
Report the numbers of the steps where you played something other than the given notes (or nothing).
